summary: This document extends DLEP with a credit window scheme aware of IEEE 802.1Q for Ethernet, supporting destination-specific and shared flow control. It builds on the base DLEP credit window mechanism.

plainLanguage.summary: DLEP is the protocol a router and a modem use to exchange information about the link between them. This document adds a way for the modem to say how much traffic the router may send, and for the two of them to agree which traffic each allowance covers. The traffic is identified by the priority and virtual network fields that Ethernet frames carry, so a separate allowance can be set for each combination.

questions: what is dlep ethernet credit extension
how does dlep flow control work
subtitle: How DLEP modems and routers can meter Ethernet traffic with credit windows tied to VLANs and priority bits.

tldr.problem: The Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol lets a modem and a router share link information, but it defines no way to control the rate at which traffic flows from the router to the modem. When the modem is the bottleneck, the router needs to be told how much it may send.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9895 builds on the DLEP traffic classification and credit window extensions and adds matching based on the IEEE 802.1Q tag. A modem advertises credit windows and the classification that maps traffic to them, and the router sends only while credits remain. The credit windows can be shared across flows or dedicated to one destination, VLAN or priority code point.
tldr.outcome: The document registers a new DLEP extension type, 5, for the IEEE 802.1Q Aware Credit Window, and states the rules for declaring it, configuring the mapping and handling a modem that advertises more windows than the router can use.

today: RFC 9895 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2026, and it has not been obsoleted. IANA has assigned the extension type code point 5 in the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol Parameters registry group. It builds on the DLEP traffic classification and credit window extensions of RFC 9892 and RFC 9893.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol is defined in RFC 8175 and provides the exchange of link-related control information between DLEP peers. DLEP peers consist of a modem and a router. DLEP defines a base set of mechanisms as well as support for possible extensions, and this document defines one such extension.

The DLEP specification does not define any flow control mechanisms. While in theory various flow control techniques could be implemented with DLEP, this document specifies a DLEP extension that introduces an Ethernet-based flow control mechanism for traffic transmitted from a router to a modem. This mechanism utilizes one or more logical credit windows, each of which is typically associated with a virtual or physical queue. The router uses the traffic flow classification information provided by the modem to determine the appropriate credit window for a given traffic flow. Credit windows may be shared across multiple flows or used on a per-flow basis. For a Diffserv-based approach to credit window flow control, the reader is referred to RFC 9894. As specified in Section 2.3.1 of RFC 9892, when both Diffserv and Ethernet traffic classification are applied to a flow, Ethernet-based classification takes precedence.

This document leverages the traffic classification and credit window flow control mechanisms defined in RFC 9892 and RFC 9893 to enable credit-window-based flow control based on DLEP destinations, Ethernet Virtual Local Area Networks, and Priority Code Points. Ethernet PCP support is specified as part of the IEEE 802.1Q tag format, which includes a 3-bit PCP field, and the tag format also incorporates a 12-bit VLAN Identifier field.

The defined mechanism allows credit windows to be shared across traffic destined for multiple DLEP destinations, VLANs and PCPs, or to be dedicated exclusively to traffic associated with a specific destination, VLAN or priority code point. The extension also supports wildcard matching for any PCP or VID. The extension is referred to as the IEEE 802.1Q Aware Credit Window, or more simply the Ethernet Credit extension.
sections.plainLanguage: A credit window is an allowance to send a certain amount of data. The modem decides how many windows it has, the router decides which window each flow belongs to, and the router sends only while an allowance remains. This document decides that the flow is identified by the fields in the Ethernet frame's tag: the three-bit priority code point that says how urgent the frame is, and the twelve-bit identifier that says which virtual network it belongs to.

sections.title: Extension Usage and Identification
sections.content:
The extension defined in this document is built on the mechanisms and processing defined in RFC 9892 and RFC 9893. To indicate that the IEEE 802.1Q Aware Credit Window Extension is to be used, an implementation must include the extension type value in the Extensions Supported Data Item of RFC 8175. The Extensions Supported Data Item is sent and processed according to RFC 8175. Any implementation that indicates the use of the extension must support all message types, Data Items, the Ethernet Traffic Classification Sub-Data Item, and all related processing defined in RFC 9892 and RFC 9893.

The IEEE 802.1Q Aware Credit Window Extension Type value is 5.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends have to agree to use this before anything is exchanged. The router announces at session start that it supports the extension, by listing the extension type in the data item that lists supported extensions. Once it has said so, it has to handle everything the underlying DLEP extensions define, not just the parts it finds useful.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content:
If this extension is supported, that support must be declared using the Extensions Supported Data Item, which is configurable on both modems and routers. Diffserv Aware Credit Window Extension Data Items must not be emitted by a DLEP participant unless such support was specified in the initialization message received from its peer. The use of the extension defined in this document should be configurable on both modems and routers.

Modems should support the configuration of mapping a priority code point to a credit window. Modems may support the configuration of mapping a priority code point to a credit window on a per-VLAN basis. The VID value zero is used by RFC 9892 to indicate that the VID is ignored, the VID 0xFFFF is reserved, and any other value from 0x0001 through 0xFFFE can be used in traffic classification. When VLANs are supported by a modem without support from PCPs, the modem should support the configuration of mapping a VLAN to a credit window. Modems may support the configuration of the number of credit windows that they advertise to a router.

Routers may impose limitations on the number of queues they can support and on the allowable credit window configurations, and in some cases per-destination queues may not be supported. If the credit window information provided by the modem exceeds the router's capabilities, the router should use a subset of the advertised credit windows. Alternatively, the router may reset the session and indicate that the extension is not supported. In either case, a mismatch in capabilities should be reported to the user through standard network management mechanisms, such as user interface notifications or error logging. Regardless of implementation, if credit windows are in use, the router must not send traffic to the modem unless sufficient credits are available.
sections.plainLanguage: The configuration decides which flows share an allowance. A modem should be able to map a priority to a window, and where VLANs are supported it should be able to map a VLAN to a window as well. A router may be able to handle fewer windows than the modem offers, in which case it uses what it can and tells the operator about the mismatch. The one rule that always applies is that the router sends nothing when there is no credit left.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document defines a DLEP extension that uses DLEP mechanisms and the credit window flow control mechanisms defined in RFC 9892 and RFC 9893. The defined extension is exposed to vulnerabilities similar to existing DLEP messages and discussed in the Security Considerations section of RFC 8175, such as an injected message resizing a credit window to a value that results in a denial of service. The security mechanisms documented in RFC 8175 can be applied equally to the mechanism defined in this document.

Wildcards for matching PCP and VID fields are provided. Note that wildcards may be convenient for matching a number of packet flows but could inadvertently match unexpected flows, or new flows that appear after the wildcard matching has been set up. It is therefore recommended that wildcards not be used unless clearly needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The same care applies as for the rest of DLEP: an injected message could resize a credit window and cause a denial of service, and the protections DLEP already defines are used here too. The document also warns about the wildcard setting: a rule that matches any priority or any virtual network will also catch flows that nobody expected it to catch, including ones that appear later, so wildcards should be used only when they are clearly needed.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has assigned the code point 5 in the Extension Type Values registry of the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol Parameters registry group to the IEEE 802.1Q Aware Credit Window.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks IANA to record the extension type number that a router lists when it says it supports this feature, so that modems and routers agree on one number.

viz.caption: The terms the extension builds on

items.title: Credit window
items.text: An allowance to send a certain amount of data, usually tied to one queue.

items.title: Traffic classification
items.text: Information the modem provides so the router can tell which credit window a flow belongs to.

items.title: Priority Code Point
items.text: The three-bit field in the IEEE 802.1Q tag that carries the priority of an Ethernet frame.

items.title: VLAN Identifier
items.text: The twelve-bit field in the IEEE 802.1Q tag that names the virtual network the frame belongs to.

items.title: Wildcard
items.text: A setting that matches any priority code point or any VLAN identifier.
